title: Irregular verbs: to be, to go, to give, to go up

objectives.can: Recognise the forms of הֲוָה, אֲזַל and הֲלַךְ, יְהַב and נְתַן, סְלִק, and אֲתָה in its causative.

explanation.summary: A handful of very common verbs do not keep to one set of forms. For 'go' and 'give' the Aramaic of the Bible draws the forms of one meaning from two different roots; for 'come up' it does the same between the Peal and the causative. These are the verbs that turn up on almost every page, so each is worth learning as a small set of forms.

sections.heading: The verb 'to be'
body: The corpus files the verb 'be, become, come to pass' under the headword הָוָא. It has only three conjugations in the texts: the perfect, the imperfect and the imperative. It has no participle and no infinitive. (The word for 'there is', which stands for 'be' in the present, is a different kind of word and not a verb in these tables.)

The perfect is regular for a final-weak verb, and it keeps the ו as a consonant before endings: the third masculine singular is הֲוָה or הֲוָא, the third feminine singular הֲוָת, the third masculine plural הֲווֹ, the first singular הֲוֵית, the second masculine singular הֲוַיְתָ. The imperfect is unusual. The third person begins with ל, not י: לֶהֱוֵא 'he will be', לֶהֱוֺן 'they will be', לֶהֶוְיָן (feminine plural). The feminine singular has ת, as in the regular verb: תֶּהֱוֵא 'she will be'. The imperative is הֱווֹ 'be!' (plural).

Its commonest use is not 'be' but a helper. The perfect or imperfect of הָוָא with a participle makes a compound tense (A4.1.3): חָזֵה הֲוַיְתָ means 'you were watching'. In those clauses the forms of הָוָא tell you the time and the participle tells you what was happening.

The paradigm tables of this lesson show what occurs as bare words, and they have gaps. For the imperfect of הָוָא they hold only the third person, singular and plural; the feminine forms and the first and second persons are not shown. For the perfect of יְהַב they hold the third masculine singular and the second masculine singular only. For the imperfect of נְתַן there are the second masculine singular and the third masculine singular and plural, and no first person. For the Haphel perfect of אָתָה there are only the third masculine singular and plural. A dash means that the texts do not have the form, not that it cannot exist.

sections.heading: The verb 'to go': אֲזַל, הוּךְ and הֲלַךְ
body: 'Go' is made from three roots. The Peal perfect, the imperative and the participle come from אֲזַל: אֲזַל 'he went' (perfect), אֲזַלוּ 'they went', אֲזַלְנָא 'we went', אֵזֶל 'go!' and the participle אֲזַל 'going'. The Peal imperfect and infinitive come from the root the corpus files under the headword הוּךְ: יְהָךְ 'he will go' and לִמְהָךְ 'to go'. The causative and the intensive stems come from הֲלַךְ: the Aphel participle מַהְלְכִין 'walking' (Daniel 3:25) and the Pael participle מְהַלֵּךְ 'walking about'.

The reason is that Aramaic did not fill the whole pattern of 'go' from one root. A learner should therefore not hunt for a perfect of הוּךְ, or an imperfect of אֲזַל, because the texts do not have them. Of these three headwords, the corpus has 7 forms of אֲזַל, 4 of הוּךְ and 3 of הֲלַךְ, so each can be learned as a short list.

sections.heading: The verb 'to give': יְהַב and נְתַן
body: 'Give' is made from two roots. The Peal perfect, the imperative and the participle come from יְהַב: יְהַב 'he gave', יְהַבְתְּ 'you gave', וִיהַבוּ 'and they gave', הַב 'give!', יָהֵב 'giving', יָהֲבִין 'giving' (plural). The Peal imperfect and infinitive come from נְתַן: יִנְתֵּן 'he will give', תִּנְתֵּן 'you will give', יִנְתְּנוּן 'they will give', יִתְּנִנַּהּ 'he will give it' and לְמִנְתַּן 'to give'. One form in the texts, יְהַב in Daniel 5:18, is tagged as an imperfect. It stands in a past narrative and has the spelling of the perfect, so do not take it as evidence that יְהַב has an imperfect.

The passive stems of 'give' come from יְהַב. The Peil is יְהִיב 'was given', יְהִיבַת (feminine) and וִיהִיבוּ (plural); the Hithpeel is יִתְיְהִב 'will be given', מִתְיְהֵב 'being given'. Because יְהַב begins with י, a Hithpeel keeps the י after the prefix. The corpus has no passive of נְתַן.

The same split occurs in the verb 'be able', for which the texts use two headwords: יְכֵל, with a perfect (יְכֵלְתָּ), an imperfect (יוּכַל) and a participle (יָכְלִין), and כְּהַל, which occurs only in the participle (כָּהֵל, כָהֲלִין). Both mean 'be able' and both are followed by an infinitive or by a clause.

sections.heading: The verb 'to go up': סְלִק and נְסַק
body: The corpus files 'go up, come up' under two headwords. סְלִק has the Peal: סְלִקוּ 'they came up' (perfect plural), סִלְקָת (feminine singular) and the participle סָלְקָן (feminine plural). The causative stems are filed under נְסַק: the Haphel perfect הַסִּקוּ 'they took up', the Haphel infinitive לְהַנְסָקָה 'to take up', and the Hophal וְהֻסַּק 'and he was taken up'. The ס of הַסִּקוּ is doubled, while in לְהַנְסָקָה a נ shows between the prefix and the root.

Some grammars treat these as two roots with one sense, and others as a single verb with the Peal and the causative drawn from different roots. The texts support either account; what they require of the reader is only to know that a causative or passive of 'go up' will be found under נְסַק.

sections.heading: The verb 'to come' and its causative
body: The Peal of 'come' is regular for a final-weak verb, and the corpus files it under אָתָה: אֲתָא or אֲתָה 'he came', אֲתוֹ 'they came', the participle אָתֵה, the imperative וֶאֱתוֹ 'and come!' and the infinitive לְמֵתֵא 'to come'.

Its causative is the usual way to say 'bring'. The Haphel has a י after the ה: הַיְתִי 'he brought', הַיְתִיו 'they brought', and the infinitive לְהַיְתָיָה 'to bring'. The Hophal is the passive: הֵיתָיוּ 'they were brought', וְהֵיתָיִת (feminine singular) 'and it was brought'. These forms are not like a strong Haphel or Hophal, because the root is weak at both ends.

misunderstandings: Do not expect a full set of forms for each of these verbs. The texts have no participle of הָוָא, no perfect of נְתַן and no imperfect of אֲזַל. A missing form is simply absent from the texts.
The ל of לֶהֱוֵא is not the preposition 'to'. It is the person letter of the imperfect of הָוָא, used for the third person.
A different headword does not mean a different meaning. אֲזַל and הוּךְ both mean 'go'; יְהַב and נְתַן both mean 'give'; the choice of root follows the conjugation.
The י of הַיְתִי is a root letter of אָתָה. It is not the person letter of an imperfect, because הַיְתִי is a perfect.

deeper.heading: Suppletion in the Semitic languages
body: Verbs that borrow forms from another root are called suppletive. 'Go' and 'give' are the standard examples in Aramaic, and the same split can be found in other Semitic languages. One view is that the two roots were once separate verbs with a close sense, and each one was kept for the part of the pattern in which it was most useful. Whatever the history, the learner has the same practical task: to identify the headword the form belongs to, and to know which conjugations that headword supplies.

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: Thou sawest till that a stone was cut out without hands, which smote the image upon its feet that were of iron and clay, and broke them to pieces.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: חָזֵה (0) is the Peal participle of 'see' and הֲוַיְתָ (1) is the Peal perfect of הָוָא, second masculine singular, 'you were'. Together they say 'you were watching': the verb 'be' gives the time, and the participle gives the action. This compound is the subject of A4.1.3. The perfect of 'be' keeps its ו as a consonant before the ending -תָ.

quoted.title: Ezra
quoted.english: I make a decree, that all they of the people of Israel, and their priests and the Levites, in my realm, that are minded of their own free will to go with thee to Jerusalem, go.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: Two forms of 'go' from the same root, הוּךְ. לִמְהָךְ (12) is the Peal infinitive with the prefix לְ-, 'to go'. יְהָךְ (15) is the Peal imperfect, third masculine singular, 'he may go'. Here 'go' is made from הוּךְ, while elsewhere the perfect, the imperative and the participle come from אֲזַל (Daniel 6:19: אֲזַל 'he went').

quoted.title: Ezra
quoted.english: And whatsoever more shall be needful for the house of thy God, which thou shalt have occasion to bestow, bestow it out of the king's treasure-house.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: לְמִנְתַּן (7) is the Peal infinitive of נְתַן, with the prefix לְ- and מִ- (A2.1.4): 'to give'. תִּנְתֵּן (8) is its Peal imperfect, second masculine singular, 'you shall give'. Both forms are from נְתַן, which supplies the infinitive and the imperfect; the perfect and imperative of 'give' come from יְהַב.

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: Therefore because the king's commandment was peremptory, and the furnace exceeding hot, the flame of the fire slew those men that took up Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed-nego.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: הַסִּקוּ is a Haphel perfect, third masculine plural, of the verb filed under נְסַק, 'they took up' (the three men). It is the causative of the Peal סְלִקוּ 'they came up' (Daniel 2:29): the Peal and the causative are filed under two headwords. The ס is doubled in הַסִּקוּ.

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: Then Nebuchadnezzar in his rage and fury commanded to bring Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed-nego. Then were these men brought before the king.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: Two forms of the causative of 'come'. לְהַיְתָיָה (5) is the Haphel infinitive with the prefix לְ-, 'to bring', which depends on the king's command. הֵיתָיוּ (13) is the Hophal perfect, third masculine plural: 'they were brought' before the king. The Haphel and the Hophal of אָתָה have the י of the root after the ה.
